newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Cyprus leaders urged to commit to negotiations.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus leaders urged to commit to negotiations.

text.p: The Security Council called on the leaders of the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities on Friday to commit themselves to a sustained process of direct negotiations, beginning with a session in New York July 9-13.
The appeal was contained in a resolution renewing until December 31, 1997, the 1,200-member U.N. Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP), deployed on the isalnd since 1964.

Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides, as head of the Greek Cypriot community, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash are to meet face-to-face for the first time in nearly three years at a rural retreat called Troutbeck 90 miles (145 kms) north of New York city.

Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since 1974 when troops from Turkey took control of the north of the island in reaction to a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece. The United Nations has been trying for years to reunite the island under a federal system.

The council resolution reiterated the long-standing U.N. view that the status quo is unacceptable. It reaffirmed that a settlement must be based on a state of Cyprus "with a single sovereignty and international personality and a single citizenship, with its independence and territorial integrity safeguarded, and comprising two politically equal communities ...in a bi-communal and bi-zonal federation."
Such a settlement must exclude union in whole or in part with any other country or any form of partition or secession.
The Turkish Cypriots proclaimed their own state in the north of the island in 1983 with Denktash as president but it is recognised only by Ankara.
The council welcomed the decision of Secretary-General Kofi Annan to launch a "sustained process of direct negotiations between the leaders of the two Cypriot communities."

It called on the leaders to "commit themselves to this process of negotiations, including participation in the first session...to be held July 9-13," and urged them to "cooperate actively and constructively with the secretary-general and his special adviser on Cyprus," former Ecuadoran Foreign Minister Diego Cordovez.
They were further urged to create a "climate for reconciliation and genuine mutual confidence" and to avoid any actions that might increase tension.

The resolution reaffirmed that a decision by the European Union concerning the opening of negotiations for Cypriot membership was "an important development that should facilitate an overall settlement." The EU talks are expected to get under way during the first half of 1998.

The council reiterated previously expressed concern at the "continuing excessive levels of military forces and armaments" in Cyprus -- a reference to the continued presence of some 30,000 Turkish troops in the north and an arms build-up in the south. The Nicosia government announced plans earlier this year to buy Russian-made S-300 air defence missiles, scheduled for delivery in 1998.
